error_modes.label: Arrival accuracy in DME at the target fix

texts.0: SP, due to a fix-to-fix solution built on a mis-read present DME, did not arrive at the target fix within the published distance tolerance. The aircraft crossed the fix more than 6 DME off, and the error was still increasing when the IP took the aircraft to re-establish the point-to-point leg. SP did not recognize the divergence from the tuned DME readout at any stage of the transition.
texts.1: SP, due to a single distance solution computed at the start and never revised, did not correct the closure error while the fix-to-fix leg was flown. Arrival distance reached the 4 DME limit of the standard and was reduced only after the IP verbally prompted a recheck of the DME. The correction was applied late and the aircraft stabilized on the fix well after the intended arrival point.
texts.2: SP, due to a coarse first estimate of the distance to run, did not fly the initial transition heading accurately enough to close the fix on the computed profile. Arrival distance opened to about 3 DME from the target fix, between the 2 and 4 DME values of the standard. SP identified the trend on the DME readout in time and closed the error without any IP input.
texts.3: SP computed the distance to the target fix from the DME and flew the transition heading that resolved it. Arrival was inside 2 DME of the fix throughout the leg, with the residual error taken out early and the DME readout used as the primary reference. The solution was reached quickly and without hesitation.
texts.4: SP resolved the fix-to-fix distance problem immediately and flew the leg so that the DME error never exceeded about 1 mile. Arrival over the target fix was essentially exact, with the distance to run reducing at the rate the solution predicted. No re-solution of the problem was required at any point.
texts.marginal: SP arrived at the target fix inside the published distance tolerance, but the DME error sat close to the 2 DME edge of the standard for most of the leg rather than reducing steadily. The trend was toward the outer limit and was arrested only in the last portion of the transition. SP is expected to tighten the running distance check so the arrival error reduces progressively rather than late.

error_modes.label: Arrival accuracy expressed in radials
error_modes.source: specific:The parameter above (distance) can be expressed in radials

texts.0: SP, due to an incorrect identification of the radial through the target fix, did not arrive on the required bearing from the station. The aircraft crossed the fix more than 6 degrees off the target radial, with no trend toward the correct one, and the IP intervened to re-establish the geometry. SP did not use the bearing pointer to detect that the fix was being approached from the wrong side.
texts.1: SP, due to a transition heading held without any reassessment of the radial being crossed, did not correct the angular error as the fix was approached. The arrival radial error reached the 4 degree limit of the standard and was reduced only after verbal prompting from the IP. The aircraft settled on the correct radial after the intended arrival point.
texts.2: SP, due to a rounded estimate of the angular difference between the present position and the target fix, did not fly the transition heading precisely enough to arrive on the required radial. The error grew to about 3 degrees, between the 2 and 4 degree values of the standard, before SP recognized the bearing trend and adjusted heading without IP input. The fix was then crossed on the correct radial.
texts.3: SP identified the radial through the target fix and flew the transition so that the angular error stayed within 2 degrees. The bearing pointer was used continuously to confirm that the aircraft was closing the correct radial. Arrival over the fix was on the required bearing without a late correction.
texts.4: SP resolved the geometry in radials at once and held the arrival bearing to within about 1 degree of the target radial. The bearing pointer tracked to the fix with no correction of consequence required. The angular solution and the distance solution converged on the same arrival point.
texts.marginal: SP arrived on the target radial within the published tolerance, but the angular error stayed near the 2 degree edge of the standard and was corrected in one late step rather than progressively. The bearing pointer was checked at intervals long enough to let the error accumulate. SP is expected to shorten the interval between bearing checks so the radial error is contained earlier in the transition.

error_modes.label: Timeliness of taking the transition heading

texts.0: SP, due to an attempt to complete the whole fix-to-fix computation before making any control input, did not take the transition heading in time. The aircraft continued on the previous heading for a large part of the available distance, so that the computed solution no longer applied when it was finally flown, and the IP directed the turn. The point-to-point leg had to be re-planned from a new present position.
texts.1: SP, due to hesitation over which of two candidate headings to fly, did not turn onto the transition heading at the point the solution required. The delay consumed enough of the leg to bring the arrival error to the limit of the standard, and the turn was started only after the IP prompted. SP then flew the heading correctly but from a position that no longer supported an accurate arrival.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow first computation of the transition heading, did not begin the turn immediately when the point-to-point was directed. The turn was started several seconds late and the resulting arrival error remained between the code 3 and code 1 values of the standard. SP recognized the delay, applied a corrected heading in good time and closed the fix without IP input.
texts.3: SP took the transition heading in time, turning onto the computed heading as soon as the point-to-point was directed. The initial solution was produced quickly enough that no distance was wasted on the previous heading. The aircraft was established on the fix-to-fix leg without delay.
texts.4: SP had the transition heading available almost immediately and rolled onto it with no measurable delay. The turn was made at a rate that put the aircraft on the computed track without overshoot. The whole entry to the point-to-point leg was completed as one continuous action.
texts.marginal: SP took the transition heading within an acceptable time, but the turn was consistently started at the late end of what the solution allowed, leaving little margin for later refinement. The delay did not by itself produce a deviation on this sortie. SP is expected to produce the first heading solution faster so the turn begins as the point-to-point is directed.

error_modes.label: Continuous recomputation and timely correction en route

texts.0: SP, due to treating the initial transition heading as fixed for the whole leg, did not calculate the correct heading continuously during the transition. The geometry changed as the aircraft moved, the deviation grew past the outer values of the standard, and the IP had to intervene to re-solve the problem and regain the fix. No intermediate solution was attempted between the start of the leg and the intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan that returned to the navigation display only at long intervals, did not correct the developing deviation in time. The recomputation was made only after the IP pointed out the divergence, and by then the error was at the limit of the standard. The corrected heading was accurate but applied too late to restore the planned arrival.
texts.2: SP, due to recomputing the heading in large steps rather than continuously, did not keep the solution matched to the changing geometry throughout the leg. The deviation opened to a value between the code 3 and code 1 limits before the next update was made. SP detected the trend, applied an intermediate correction in good time and arrived without IP input.
texts.3: SP recalculated the required heading continuously as the geometry changed and corrected the small deviations as they appeared. Each update was applied in time, so the error was held inside the code 3 values for the whole transition. No single large correction was needed near the fix.
texts.4: SP updated the fix-to-fix solution smoothly throughout the leg, so that heading changes were small and made before any deviation became visible. The aircraft tracked to the fix as if flown on a single computed course. The arrival required no correction at all in the final portion.
texts.marginal: SP recalculated the heading during the transition and stayed within standards, but the updates came in a few discrete steps and each was applied at the point where the deviation had already become noticeable. The technique worked on this leg and would not have tolerated a shorter distance to run. SP is expected to move to a continuous update of the solution rather than periodic re-solutions.

error_modes.label: Knowledge of the standardized fix-to-fix solution method
error_modes.hf_concept: insufficient knowledge of the published procedure

texts.0: SP, due to lack of knowledge of the published procedure for the condition encountered, did not solve the point-to-point problem according to the standardized method of the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3. The heading produced was not derived from the present position and target fix geometry, the resulting error exceeded the outer values of the standard, and the IP took the aircraft and demonstrated the solution. SP could not state the steps of the method when questioned in flight.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete knowledge of the standardized fix-to-fix sequence, did not apply the steps in the correct order and produced a heading with a systematic error. The deviation reached the limit of the standard and was resolved only after the IP talked SP through the method step by step. SP flew the corrected heading accurately once it had been supplied.
texts.2: SP, due to a partially recalled version of the standardized method, did not apply one step of the solution correctly and produced a heading that was close but not exact. The arrival error stayed between the code 3 and code 1 values of the standard. SP recognized that the geometry did not match the expected picture, reworked the solution correctly and completed the leg without IP input.
texts.3: SP solved the fix-to-fix problem by the standardized method described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3, with the steps applied in the correct order. The heading produced was correct for the geometry and no IP intervention was required. SP was able to state the reasoning behind the solution when asked.
texts.4: SP applied the standardized point-to-point method flawlessly and produced the correct heading without any intermediate working being visible in the flight path. The method was used identically on each repetition, including the case where the fix lay behind the aircraft. SP explained the solution accurately and immediately when questioned.
texts.marginal: SP solved the problem by the standardized method and stayed within the published values, but the working was slow and one step was reconstructed rather than recalled. Knowledge of the method was sufficient for this geometry and would be thin under a shorter distance to run. SP is expected to consolidate the published sequence so the solution is produced without reconstruction.

error_modes.label: Wind and groundspeed accounting on the point-to-point leg

texts.0: SP, due to a solution computed without any allowance for the known wind, did not correct the drift that developed along the fix-to-fix leg. The aircraft was displaced progressively downwind, the arrival error exceeded the outer values of the standard in both distance and radial, and the IP intervened to re-establish the track. SP did not compare the actual bearing trend with the trend the no-wind solution predicted.
texts.1: SP, due to a drift correction estimated once and never revised against the observed bearing change, did not keep the aircraft on the computed track. The displacement built up to the limit of the standard and was corrected only after the IP called attention to the bearing pointer. The final part of the leg was flown with a large drift correction that had to be removed again near the fix.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial drift allowance that was smaller than the actual wind required, did not hold the computed track through the first part of the transition. The error opened to a value between the code 3 and code 1 limits before SP compared the observed and expected bearing rates. The drift correction was then increased in good time and the fix was made without IP input.
texts.3: SP allowed for the wind in the transition heading and adjusted the drift correction as the observed bearing rate indicated. The aircraft held the computed track and arrived at the fix inside the code 3 values in both distance and radial. Groundspeed was used to confirm the time and distance to run.
texts.4: SP incorporated the wind into the solution from the outset and refined the drift correction by very small amounts as the bearing rate confirmed it. The track to the fix stayed effectively straight and the arrival error was negligible. Groundspeed and distance to run agreed throughout the leg.
texts.marginal: SP allowed for drift and remained within the published values, but the correction was set from the forecast wind and adjusted only once against what the instruments showed. The residual displacement stayed near the edge of the code 3 band for part of the leg. SP is expected to derive the drift correction from the observed bearing rate rather than relying on the pre-flight wind.

error_modes.label: Instrument cross-check and aircraft control while solving the problem

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on the navigation display at the expense of the instrument cross-check, did not maintain the aircraft state while working the point-to-point problem. Attitude, altitude and heading were left unmonitored long enough for the flight path to diverge, and the IP took the aircraft. The navigation solution was also not completed, so both the flying and the problem were lost together.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention remained on the fix-to-fix computation, did not keep the primary flight parameters under control during the transition. The deviation reached the limit of the standard and was recovered only after the IP called for a return to the basic scan. SP then flew the aircraft accurately but had to restart the navigation solution.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that dwelt on the navigation display while the problem was being worked, did not cross-check the primary flight instruments at the required rate. Heading and altitude drifted enough to place the arrival error between the code 3 and code 1 values of the standard. SP recognized the narrowed scan, re-established the cross-check and corrected the deviation without IP input.
texts.3: SP kept the instrument cross-check running while solving the point-to-point problem, so that attitude, altitude and heading were held throughout the transition. The navigation work was fitted into the scan rather than replacing it. The fix was made inside the code 3 values with the aircraft state stable.
texts.4: SP worked the fix-to-fix solution without any detectable interruption of the instrument cross-check. The primary flight parameters were held essentially constant while the heading updates were computed and applied. Aircraft control and navigation were carried out as a single integrated task.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft within standards while solving the problem, but the cross-check narrowed toward the navigation display each time a new heading was computed, and the primary parameters moved slightly before being recaptured. Capacity was adequate for this workload and left little margin for an added task. SP is expected to keep the basic scan running continuously while the point-to-point solution is worked.

error_modes.label: GPS/RNAV direct-to-fix setup and mode management

texts.0: SP, due to mode confusion over the selected navigation source and what it was displaying, did not set up the direct-to-fix navigation correctly for the assigned point. The aircraft was flown toward a waypoint other than the one required and the resulting error was far outside the published values before the IP intervened and reselected the correct fix. SP did not cross-check the GPS/RNAV picture against the VOR/DME or TACAN raw data at any stage.
texts.1: SP, due to acceptance of the automated solution without an independent check of the parameters, did not verify that the direct-to entry matched the fix that had been assigned. The discrepancy was identified only after the IP questioned the displayed track, by which time the error was at the limit of the standard. SP corrected the entry and flew the leg accurately from that point.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow and partly incorrect sequence in entering the direct-to fix, did not complete the RNAV setup before the transition heading was required. The first part of the leg was flown on an approximate heading and the arrival error stayed between the code 3 and code 1 values. SP completed the entry, cross-checked it against the raw data and refined the heading without IP input.
texts.3: SP set up the direct-to-fix navigation for the assigned point correctly and confirmed it against the VOR/DME or TACAN raw data before turning. The selected mode and the displayed track were identified before they were used to fly the aircraft. The fix was made inside the code 3 values of the standard.
texts.4: SP configured the RNAV direct-to fix immediately and verified the entry, the active mode and the raw-data picture as one check. The transition heading was flown from a solution that the GPS and the ground-based aids both supported. No reselection or re-entry was needed at any point in the leg.
texts.marginal: SP set up the direct-to-fix navigation correctly and remained within the published values, but the entry was verified against the raw data only after the turn had been started. The cross-check confirmed rather than preceded the action. SP is expected to confirm the selected fix and mode against the raw data before flying the computed heading.

error_modes.label: Reading present position and target fix on the EHSI

texts.0: SP, due to an incorrect mental model of the EHSI picture, did not place the present position between the tail of the bearing pointer and the centre of the display and the target fix between the centre and the head of the course arrow. The two positions were interchanged, so the heading taken was on the wrong side of the geometry and the aircraft tracked away from the fix. The distance error passed 4 DME and the IP took over the navigation to re-establish the leg.
texts.1: SP, due to confusing which side of the EHSI centre held the present position and which held the target fix, did not build the fix-to-fix picture as the manual describes. The first heading was taken from the reversed picture and only the IP prompt about the tail of the bearing pointer led SP to rebuild it. Arrival on the target radial was at the 4 DME limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a momentary reversal of the tail of the bearing pointer and the head of the course arrow when building the EHSI picture, did not select the correct side of the geometry on the first attempt. The wrong-sided heading was flown briefly and produced an error between 2 and 4 DME. SP rechecked the display, identified the present position correctly and corrected in good time without IP input.
texts.3: SP identified the present position between the tail of the bearing pointer and the centre of the EHSI, and the target fix between the centre and the head of the course arrow, before selecting any heading. The picture was built correctly the first time and the fix was made within 2 DME of the target. No reversal of the two positions occurred during the leg.
texts.4: SP read the EHSI picture without hesitation, placing present position and target fix on their correct sides of the display each time the geometry was reassessed. Every heading came from a correct picture and the arrival deviation stayed at a fraction of a mile. The interpretation was consistent from the first construction to the fix.
texts.marginal: SP placed the present position and the target fix correctly on the EHSI, but needed a second look at the tail of the bearing pointer before committing to a heading on more than one update. Arrival remained inside 2 DME. SP is expected to fix the relative positions on the display at first glance so no distance is lost re-reading the picture.

error_modes.label: Tune, identify and monitor of the NAVAID before the fix-to-fix

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the tune, identify and monitor sequence on the NAVAID, did not double check that the correct frequency was selected before starting the fix-to-fix. The radial and DME used in the solution came from a different station, the whole geometry was therefore false and the aircraft was flown outside the 4 DME limit of the standard. The IP identified the station and reset the frequency.
texts.1: SP, due to selecting the frequency without identifying and monitoring the station, did not confirm that the displayed radial and DME belonged to the intended NAVAID. The wrong selection was found only after the IP asked for the identifier, and the distance lost while verifying it left the arrival at the 4 DME limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a late identification of the NAVAID, did not have the raw data confirmed at the moment the point-to-point was directed. The first part of the leg was flown on unverified information and the arrival error stayed between 2 and 4 DME. SP identified and monitored the station in time to rebuild the solution and closed the fix without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP tuned, identified and monitored the NAVAID and double checked the selected frequency before setting up the fix-to-fix. All radial and DME information used in the solution came from the confirmed station and the fix was made within 2 DME. The identifier was left monitored for the whole leg.
texts.4: SP completed the tune, identify and monitor sequence and the frequency double check as part of the normal flow, with no interruption to the navigation problem. The solution was built entirely on verified raw data and the arrival deviation was negligible. Station identification was rechecked without prompting when the leg was extended.
texts.marginal: SP tuned, identified and monitored the correct NAVAID, but the frequency double check was completed after the first heading had already been taken. No information from a wrong station was used and arrival stayed inside 2 DME. SP is expected to finish the identification and the double check before any part of the fix-to-fix solution is flown.

error_modes.label: Setting the target radial in the course selector window

texts.0: SP, due to setting the reciprocal of the target radial in the course selector window, did not place the course arrow where the fix-to-fix picture requires. The heading was then taken toward a point on the opposite side of the station and the distance error grew past 4 DME before the IP corrected the CSW setting. The error was not caught by any comparison with the assigned fix.
texts.1: SP, due to setting the course selector window from memory instead of from the assigned fix, did not have the correct radial displayed when the initial heading was taken. The course arrow was several degrees off the target radial and the setting was corrected only after the IP pointed at the CSW, leaving arrival on the radial at the 4 degree limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried entry in the course selector window, did not check the set value against the assigned radial before turning. The small mis-set of the course arrow biased the first heading and produced an error between 2 and 4 degrees on the target radial. SP noticed the discrepancy against the raw data, reset the CSW and corrected the heading in good time.
texts.3: SP set the radial of the desired fix in the course selector window and confirmed it against the assignment before turning. The course arrow gave the correct reference for the whole solution and the target radial was crossed within 2 degrees of the assigned value.
texts.4: SP set the course selector window to the target radial immediately after the fix was assigned and confirmed the displayed value without prompting. The reference used for every heading update was exactly the assigned radial and the arrival deviation was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP set the correct radial in the course selector window, but only after the initial turn had begun, using the bearing pointer alone for the first heading. Arrival stayed within 2 degrees of the target radial. SP is expected to set and confirm the CSW before taking any heading toward the fix.

error_modes.label: Initial heading between the pointer heads and the DME favouring rule

texts.0: SP, due to disregarding the rule that the initial heading lies between the head of the bearing pointer and the head of the course arrow, did not turn to a heading inside that sector. The turn was also made in the longer direction, so the aircraft pointed outside the geometry for a large part of the leg and the distance error exceeded 4 DME before the IP directed a new heading.
texts.1: SP, due to taking the plain midpoint heading with no allowance for the destination DME being smaller than the present DME, did not favour the head of the bearing pointer as the technique requires. The aircraft reached the target radial well outside the required distance, at the 4 DME limit of the standard, and only after the IP had prompted for a correction.
texts.2: SP, due to applying the favouring rule only in part, did not bias the initial heading far enough toward the head of the course arrow with the destination DME greater than the present DME. The under-biased heading produced an arrival error between 2 and 4 DME. SP recognized the trend at the first update and applied the correct bias in good time.
texts.3: SP turned in the shorter direction to a heading between the head of the bearing pointer and the head of the course arrow, favouring the correct one for the DME relationship. The initial heading put the aircraft on a usable track from the start and the fix was made within 2 DME.
texts.4: SP selected the initial heading inside the sector between the two pointer heads with the bias sized exactly as the DME relationship required, and rolled out in the shorter direction. Only minor refinement was needed afterwards and the arrival deviation was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP turned in the shorter direction to a heading between the two pointer heads, but the bias toward the favoured head was smaller than the DME difference called for. Arrival stayed inside 2 DME because the later updates absorbed the difference. SP is expected to size the initial bias to the DME relationship so the first heading needs less refinement.

error_modes.label: Ratio construction for a target DME different from the present DME

texts.0: SP, due to using only the no-wind midpoint heading, did not apply the construction that places arrival at twice or at one half of the present DME. With the target fix at half the present distance the aircraft reached the target radial more than 4 DME from the required distance and the IP had to re-solve the problem. SP could not state the midway construction when questioned.
texts.1: SP, due to a misapplied ratio, did not take the heading midway between the midpoint and the head of the course arrow with the target DME about twice the present DME. The heading taken fell close to the plain midpoint, and after IP prompting the arrival was at the 4 DME limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to an approximate reading of the heading midway between the midpoint and the head of the bearing pointer, did not aim accurately at a target at half the present DME. The arrival error was between 2 and 4 DME. SP rebuilt the construction at the next update and corrected before reaching the radial.
texts.3: SP applied the ratio construction correctly, taking a heading midway between the midpoint and the appropriate pointer head for the required DME relationship. Arrival on the target radial was within 2 DME of the assigned distance.
texts.4: SP used the ratio construction fluently, moving the heading inside the sector as the required DME ratio changed along the leg. The arrival deviation was negligible in both distance and radial.
texts.marginal: SP used the ratio construction and arrived within 2 DME, but the midway heading was estimated rather than referenced to the two pointer heads, and it moved noticeably between updates. SP is expected to build the ratio heading from the displayed pointer positions so successive solutions agree.

error_modes.label: Anticipating the DME decrease before the increase (cutting the arc)

texts.0: SP, due to not anticipating that with both the head of the bearing pointer and the head of the course arrow in the upper half of the EHSI the DME first decreases before increasing to the target, did not hold the computed heading while the track was cutting the arc. Repeated turns were made against the falling DME, the aircraft was driven off the solution and the arrival error exceeded 4 DME before the IP intervened.
texts.1: SP, due to reading the initial DME decrease as an error in the solution, did not keep the computed heading through the part of the leg where the track cuts inside the arc. The heading was changed twice toward the station and the original solution was restored only after IP prompting, leaving arrival at the 4 DME limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to surprise at the DME decreasing after the turn, did not immediately recognize the geometry the manual describes for two pointer heads in the upper half of the display. One unnecessary heading change was made and produced an error between 2 and 4 DME, before SP identified the arc-cutting effect and returned to the computed heading in good time.
texts.3: SP anticipated that the DME would decrease before increasing toward the target and held the computed heading through that part of the leg. No correction was made against the falling distance and the fix was made within 2 DME.
texts.4: SP stated the expected DME decrease before the turn and treated the falling distance as confirmation that the solution was working. The heading was refined only for the changing geometry and the arrival deviation was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP held the computed heading while the DME decreased, but questioned the trend aloud and started to reach for a correction before accepting the geometry. Arrival stayed inside 2 DME. SP is expected to anticipate the arc-cutting effect before the turn so the falling DME is expected rather than explained afterwards.

error_modes.label: Scaling the EHSI as a map for the fix-to-fix construction

texts.0: SP, due to visualizing the EHSI without using the DME of the position furthest from the station as the distance to the outer bezel ring, did not plot the present position and the target fix at the correct radii. Both points were placed at arbitrary distances from the centre, the line construction produced a heading unrelated to the real geometry and the arrival error passed 4 DME before the IP re-solved the problem.
texts.1: SP, due to scaling the display to the present DME instead of to the greater of the two distances, did not keep the more distant point inside the compass card. The construction was compressed and the heading taken from it was in error, and after IP prompting the arrival was at the 4 DME limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a rough estimate of the two radii on the EHSI, did not place the points accurately enough for the parallel line through the centre of the compass card. The heading obtained was slightly off and the arrival error was between 2 and 4 DME, which SP identified at the next update and corrected in time.
texts.3: SP scaled the EHSI with the ground station at the centre and the furthest position on the outer ring, then took the heading from the line joining the two points transferred through the centre of the compass card. The construction was accurate and the fix was made within 2 DME.
texts.4: SP built the map picture on the EHSI at the correct scale at every update and used the parallel-line and the vertical-alignment constructions interchangeably without hesitation. The headings produced agreed with the raw data throughout and the arrival deviation was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP scaled the EHSI correctly and used the construction, but placed the two points by eye with enough spread between attempts that each update produced a slightly different heading. Arrival stayed inside 2 DME. SP is expected to hold the scale to the furthest DME so consecutive constructions agree.

error_modes.label: Updates built on current DME at scheduled ratio distances

texts.0: SP, due to repeating the solution with the DME held from the start of the leg instead of the current DME, did not obtain a valid heading from any of the updates made. Each recomputation reproduced the original geometry, the aircraft was flown on a track that no longer applied and the arrival error exceeded 4 DME before the IP intervened.
texts.1: SP, due to updating at arbitrary distances that formed no simple ratio with the target DME, did not have a usable construction ready where the geometry was changing fastest. The updates that were made used stale distances, the IP prompted for a recomputation and arrival was at the 4 DME limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to entering the current DME late into the second construction, did not take the update at the planned ratio distance. The heading was refreshed after the planned point and the resulting error stayed between 2 and 4 DME, which SP removed in good time with a further solution built on current DME.
texts.3: SP planned the updates at distances forming simple ratios with the target DME and rebuilt each solution on the current DME. The heading was refreshed at the planned points and arrival stayed within 2 DME.
texts.4: SP named the planned update distances before the turn and rebuilt the solution on current DME at each of them, so every correction was small. The heading changes required were minor throughout and the arrival deviation was negligible.
texts.marginal: SP rebuilt the solution on current DME and arrived inside 2 DME, but the updates were taken when time allowed rather than at the planned ratio distances, and the last one was left close to the fix. SP is expected to schedule the updates at distances that form simple ratios with the target DME.
